A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JEGAL study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval, gesture-word spotting and active-speaker detection experiments, ablations and qualitative results in Tables 2–7 and the appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports revised original experiments and adds robustness, modality-drop, runtime and activation-map analyses in Appendix B.

M1.justification: The stated losses in Eqs. (2) and (4) gain leading minus signs, correcting their objective formulations. The encoders, fusion, word alignment, default modality dropping and inference procedures remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.

E1.justification: Section 3.9 replaces LRS3 and LRS3-lang with MultiVSR, but its 556.1 hours, 6,934 speakers and 130,510 clips exactly match their combined totals. The source description changes and language counts disappear, leaving actual training-coverage change versus relabeling unresolved. The three tasks and AVSpeech test source remain; the new lighting/pose analyses subdivide existing AVS-Spot data.

E2.justification: Tables 2–4 retain Clip4Clip, LanguageBind, GestSync and GestureDiffuCLIP in their corresponding comparisons. The new robustness table reuses GestSync and GestureDiffuCLIP; its shortened name GestDiffuClip refers to the same cited method.

E3.justification: Table 1 revises test-set speaker counts and clip durations while retaining 500 clips per benchmark and the task metrics; AVS-Asd changes from 500 to 398 speakers and 3.80 to 3.15 seconds average duration. Added protocols include lighting/pose stratification, 30%/50%/70% modality-drop settings and five-second GPU timing. The PDFs do not explain whether the existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix B substantially extends analysis beyond the retained stress, loss and fusion studies. It tests lighting/viewpoint robustness, sensitivity to modality-drop rates, computational efficiency and spatial attention to hands. Several qualitative spotting examples are also replaced.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 newly specifies that inference time is averaged across ten runs. This concerns timing measurements; neither version reports repeated-seed accuracy estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 2–7 replace many scores and change rankings. For six-speaker detection, v1 ranks joint-modality JEGAL at 59.0 above fine-tuned GestSync at 48.0; v2 ranks GestSync at 54.4 above JEGAL at 48.0. Tables 8–10 add robustness, modality-drop and timing results. Revised dataset descriptions and test statistics prevent interpreting these replacements as controlled performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: The negative signs added to Eqs. (2) and (4) correct the mathematical losses to agree with the stated objective of favoring matching pairs. The remaining alignment and scoring definitions are retained, and no new theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: The abstract removes the qualification that JEGAL outperforms previous methods across all three tasks. The introduction changes its comparison with vision-language foundation models from outperforming them to performing on par. The task, benchmark and weakly supervised tri-modal learning contributions remain.

C2.justification: Section 5.4 now explains GestSync's detection advantage through strong frame-level supervision. Appendix B adds the limitation that bidirectional attention prevents streaming and interprets activation maps as evidence of hand focus. The limitations section removes v1's TED/TEDx training bias and conversational-generalization caveat.

D1.justification: v2 adds inference hardware, input-duration and timing details. Its appendix changes the code/model statement from a future release to a completed release, resolving inconsistency with the availability claim already present in both abstracts. Architecture specifications and training hyperparameters remain, while training-data provenance documentation is revised.

R1.justification: v2 removes the LRS3-TED and Now You're Speaking My Language references and adds Scaling Multilingual Visual Speech Recognition for MultiVSR. The broader related-work discussion and claimed distinction from existing gesture methods remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section order and most prose are retained. Local revisions affect the abstract, contribution statement, training-data description, results discussion, affiliation and acknowledgements. A new appendix analysis section shifts subsequent appendix lettering without reorganizing the overall narrative.

P2.justification: The appendix substantially expands its visual evidence with robustness, modality-drop and runtime tables, a test-diversity figure and spatial activation maps. Existing heatmaps are redrawn and several examples replaced, including every with specific. The architecture table is retained as Table 11 instead of Table 8; Figure 1's caption is corrected without adding examples.

improvement.justification: Corrected loss signs improve mathematical correctness, and Table 5's audio aggregate now agrees with Table 3. Appendix B adds useful robustness, sensitivity and efficiency evidence, while Section 5.4 acknowledges GestSync's detection lead. These gains are limited by unexplained training-data provenance changes and a new overstatement: Appendix B.2 claims 50% modality dropping is best in every inference setting, although Table 9 gives higher text-only and audio-only accuracy at 70%.
